name: Potala Palace
info: The Potala Palace is the dzong-style palace complex on Marpo Ri in Lhasa, begun in 1645 on the order of the 5th Dalai Lama, the residence of the Dalai Lamas from 1649 to 1959 and now a museum.

sections.origins:
The Potala Palace stands on Marpo Ri, the Red Hill, in the centre of the Lhasa Valley, on the site of a palace attributed to Songtsen Gampo, the first Tibetan emperor, traditionally dated to 637. Two chapels at the northwest corner of the present complex conserve parts of that earlier palace: the Phakpa Lhakhang, and the Chogyel Drupuk, a recessed cavern identified as Songtsen Gampo's meditation cave.

Ngawang Lozang Gyatso, the Great Fifth Dalai Lama, started building the present palace in 1645. One of his spiritual advisers, Konchog Chophel, the Thirty-fifth Ganden Tripa of the Gelug school, had pointed out that the site was ideal as a seat of government, lying between Drepung and Sera monasteries and the old city of Lhasa. The palace takes its name from Mount Potalaka, regarded in Buddhist tradition as the mythical abode of the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
sections.content:
The palace is built in the dzong style. It has inward-sloping walls with straight rows of windows in their upper parts and flat roofs at various levels. At the south base of the rock a large space is enclosed by walls and gates, with great porticoes on the inner side, and a series of staircases with intervals leads to the summit. The palace occupies the whole width of the rock.

The central part of the group of buildings is a quadrangle ending in gilt canopies like those of the Jokhang Temple. Its crimson central member, the Red Palace, contains the principal halls, chapels and shrines of past Dalai Lamas. The lower white frontage on the south side was used to hoist two gigantic thangkas, joined, showing Tara and Sakyamuni, during the Sertreng Festival on the 30th day of the second Tibetan month. The colours of red, white and yellow come from the application of limestone.
sections.making:
The complex rises 13 stories, reaching 119 metres above the mountain and over 300 metres above the valley floor, at an altitude of about 3,700 metres. It measures 400 metres east to west and 350 metres north to south. Its sloping stone walls average 3 metres thick and are 5 metres thick at the base, with copper poured into the foundations for earthquake protection.

The 5th Dalai Lama had moved the centre of his administration to Lhasa in 1642, with the help of Güshi Khan of the Khoshut, and Lhasa became both the religious and the political capital. Building began in 1645, after the spiritual adviser Konchog Chophel, who died in 1646, pointed out that the site lay between Drepung and Sera monasteries and overlooked Songtsen Gampo’s old capital. The Potrang Karpo, the White Palace, was completed in 1648, and in 1649 the Dalai Lama and his government moved into it. The Potala was used as a winter palace from then on.

The external structure was built in 3 years, while the interior, together with its furnishings, took 45 years. The initial phase of construction continued until 1694. The Potrang Marpo, the Red Palace, was added between 1690 and 1694. The Kalachakra Mandala was constructed during the 1690s and the Yamantaka Mandala in 1751.

The 5th Dalai Lama died in 1682, and his death was kept hidden from the general public so that the palace could be finished and to prevent Tibet’s neighbours taking advantage of a gap in the succession. This was the work of his Prime Minister, the Desi Sangye Gyatso, who carried out the wishes of the 5th Dalai Lama. People were told that he was continuing a long retreat. Meals were taken to his chamber, and on important occasions his ceremonial gown was placed on the throne. When Mongol princes insisted on an audience, an old monk of Namgyal monastery named Depa Deyab, who resembled the Dalai Lama, took his place, wearing a hat and an eye shade. Accounts differ on how long the secret was kept: some say twelve years, to 1694, others fifteen years, or until 1696.
sections.reception:
From 1649 until 1959 the Potala served as the residence of the Dalai Lamas, having been used as their winter palace from the start. Among at least one group of Tibetans around 1950 it was known colloquially as Peak Potala (Tse Potala), or most commonly as the Peak.

Its building belonged to a wider rebuilding of Lhasa. The 5th Dalai Lama, who is credited with unifying Tibet under the Ganden Phodrang, proclaimed Lhasa the capital once more, in a move that recalled Songtsen Gampo. The oldest of the city’s surviving buildings, among them parts of the Potala and the Jokhang, date to this second flowering of Lhasa, and the Jokhang Temple was also greatly expanded around the same time.

The palace complex became a museum following the annexation of Tibet by the People’s Republic of China. Its name has been explained in two ways: as that of Mount Potalaka, the mythical abode of Avalokiteśvara in Buddhist tradition, and as that of a hill on Cape Comorin at the southern tip of India, a rocky point sacred to the bodhisattva of compassion, who is also known as Chenrezi.
sections.survival:
The palace was damaged during the Tibetan uprising against the Chinese in 1959, when Chinese shells were launched into its windows. The 14th Dalai Lama fled to India during the uprising, and the government converted the palace into a museum. In 1966 it escaped damage during the Cultural Revolution through the personal intervention of Zhou Enlai, then Premier of the People’s Republic of China. Many other important sites in Lhasa were damaged or destroyed during that decade, mostly but not solely in the Cultural Revolution, and many have been restored since the 1980s.

According to the Tibetan historian Tsering Woeser, the palace, which held over 100,000 volumes of scriptures and historical documents and many store rooms of precious objects, handicrafts, paintings, wall hangings, statues and ancient armour, was almost robbed empty.

Restoration works between 1989 and 1994 cost RMB55 million. A further restoration began in 2002 at a cost of RMB180 million. UNESCO expressed concern over the materials used, while the palace’s director, Qiangba Gesang, clarified that only traditional materials and craftsmanship were used. Visits to the roof were banned after the restoration was completed in 2006, to avoid further structural damage.
sections.legacy:
The Potala was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994. The Jokhang Temple and the Norbulingka are also part of the World Heritage Site, which is called the Historic Ensemble of the Potala Palace. UNESCO has expressed concern over modern structures built immediately around the palace, which it said threaten its unique atmosphere, and, with renovation around historic sites such as the Potala, over the deterioration of Lhasa’s traditional cityscape. The Chinese government responded to the first concern with a rule barring any structure taller than 21 metres in the area.

The palace is today a museum complex in Lhasa, the capital of the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. Its Red Palace still holds the principal halls, chapels and shrines of past Dalai Lamas, and the complex contains more than 1,000 rooms, 10,000 shrines and some 200,000 statues. The 5th Dalai Lama, who built the Potala, is also remembered for the form of government he instituted, which with few changes lasted into the 1950s.

summary: The Potala Palace in Lhasa was begun in 1645 by the 5th Dalai Lama on the site of an earlier palace attributed to Songtsen Gampo. It was the Dalai Lamas' residence from 1649 to 1959 and is now a museum complex, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994.

Second pass with the articles on the 5th Dalai Lama and on Lhasa. The length of the concealment of the 5th Dalai Lama’s death differs: the Potala article says construction lasted until 1694, some twelve years after his death; the 5th Dalai Lama article says hidden "until 1696", then quotes fifteen years (and the future 6th Dalai Lama was educated until 1697). The text gives the three figures without choosing. The White Palace is "completed in 1648" (Lhasa) and occupied in 1649 (Potala, 5th Dalai Lama): both kept. The rumour that Sangye Gyatso was the Dalai Lama’s son is left out. The Potala article says Songtsen Gampo’s palace is traditionally dated 637; the Lhasa article says he raised the first structures there in 637: the traditional dating is kept.
